processes: Setting how many bonds an atom can form
plainLanguageExplanation: A valence electron is an electron that lives in the outermost shell of an atom. Think of an atom as a nesting of shells — layers — around its nucleus, like the layers of an onion. The electrons in the OUTERMOST layer are the valence electrons, and they are the ones that matter for chemistry. Here is why: when atoms react, it is always the outermost electrons that do the work. In a covalent bond, atoms share valence electrons. In an ionic bond, atoms transfer valence electrons. The electrons in the inner shells just stay put — they are not part of the action. How many valence electrons an atom has decides everything about its behavior: how many bonds it can form, whether it gives electrons away or grabs them, and how reactive it is. Sodium, with one valence electron, is eager to give it up; chlorine, with seven, is eager to grab one more. And here is the pattern: every element in the same column of the periodic table has the same number of valence electrons — which is exactly why they behave alike.

whyItMatters: Valence electrons are the single most important idea for understanding chemical bonding. They explain why the periodic table is arranged the way it is, why elements in a column behave alike, and why some atoms form one bond while others form four. Master the valence electron and you can predict how atoms will combine.
didYouKnow: Noble gases like helium and neon have full outer shells of valence electrons — which is why they almost never bond with anything at all.
compareReason: A Lewis structure is literally a drawing of valence electrons — comparing the atom's shells with its dot diagram shows how the same idea appears in two forms.
